teaching.causalExplanation: All three systems work in every session, so "aerobic" or "anaerobic" names the system that's pushed hard enough to adapt. Two things decide it, and neither is the sport's name. First, intensity: below about eighty-five per cent of maximum effort, the aerobic system leads. Second, and more often missed, the work-to-rest ratio. Earlier, you explained the six sprints. Now treat them as training. Thirty-metre sprints, about five seconds each, with three minutes' rest, is about one to thirty-six. Every sprint starts fresh, so that trains speed and power. Cut the rest to twenty seconds, one to four, and phosphocreatine never fully refills. Glycolysis takes more of the load, and now you're training repeat sprints and lactate tolerance. The rest is part of the prescription. Now compare the two kinds of training properly, one criterion at a time. Intensity: aerobic training sits at about seventy to eighty-five per cent of maximum heart rate, whereas anaerobic training goes above eighty-five per cent of maximum heart rate, often all-out. Effort: minutes to hours, against seconds to about two minutes. Work-to-rest: continuous or about one to one, against one to three up to one to twenty or more. System: aerobic, against ATP-PCr or glycolytic. Adaptations: a bigger stroke volume, more capillaries and mitochondria, against bigger fuel stores, better buffering and stronger muscles. Recovery: aerobic work can be done on consecutive days, but heavy anaerobic sessions need about forty-eight hours. And both follow the same principles, and both fade if you stop. A training method is just a way of arranging work and rest. Group them by the system they stress. For the aerobic system: continuous training, steady for twenty minutes or more; fartlek, continuous running with changes of pace; long intervals of two to five minutes; and circuits, stations with little rest. For the anaerobic systems: short intervals and repeated sprints; plyometrics, like bounding and depth jumps, for explosive power; and resistance training, for strength and muscle size.

scenes.teachingReason: Now compare the two kinds of training properly, one criterion at a time. Intensity: aerobic training sits at about seventy to eighty-five per cent of maximum heart rate, whereas anaerobic training goes above eighty-five per cent of maximum heart rate, often all-out. Recovery: aerobic work can be done on consecutive days, but heavy anaerobic sessions need about forty-eight hours. And both follow the same principles, and both fade if you stop.

scenes.teachingReason: The syllabus also asks for contemporary methods. Judge each one by what it really offers. HIIT, short near-maximal efforts with brief rests, builds aerobic and anaerobic fitness in far less time, but its recovery cost means it can't be done every day. Altitude camps can raise red blood cells, but results vary a lot. And heart rate monitors and GPS let a coach measure the load, so they can check a session did what was planned.

scenes.teachingReason: The physiology is the same for a solo runner and a team. The planning problem isn't. A runner has one event profile and one set of test results, so the coach can set an exact pace for that athlete. A squad has several positions with different demands, and a wide spread of fitness, sometimes years of growth apart. One pace for everyone is easy for the strongest and too hard for the weakest. That's training to the average. So, the twelve laps: one load for a whole spread of players, a steady run for a stop-start sport, and the same session all season. The player it nearly suits is the central midfielder, who covers the most ground at moderate pace, and even for them, it's only a base.

scenes.teachingReason: The fix is differentiation: one session that loads every athlete properly, without splitting the squad. There are four levers. Intensity, set relatively, as a percentage of each player's own maximum heart rate or best time, so the stress is equal even when the speeds aren't. Volume, the same quality but fewer repetitions, which suits a player coming back from injury. Recovery, which changes the system being trained, so it's the most powerful lever and the easiest to misuse. And role, the same structure, with conditioning that matches each position. A session pitched at the fittest player also tells everyone else they don't belong, so differentiation keeps players in the game.
